answer.answer:
Adopting a robotic process is mostly a delivery change, not a purchase: robotic assembly requires a robotic arm, but it equally requires an adapted business model and work culture, prefabrication off-site, and standardised components, and where people work alongside the machine it requires workforce training and compliance with robot safety standards. Of those requirements, only the arm is a machine; the rest sit in how the project is contracted, sequenced and staffed. The weights are very uneven: workforce training is drawn on by 44 of the 50 coded cases and standardisation by 25, while a mobile factory is drawn on by 1. The deployed Japanese records here show assembly and handling robots running at high readiness in firms that control their own production, but none of those records is linked in front of me to the enablers above, so the delivery argument rests on the literature-backed dependencies rather than on the census entries.

**What robotic assembly itself requires**

Four requirements run into PR4 "Robotic assembly", drawn on by 13 of the 50 coded cases [1]:

- Hardware. Robotic assembly dependsOn RE2 "Robotic arm" (DEP24), because robotic assembly requires a robot arm [1], peer-reviewed; RE2 is drawn on by 22 of the 50 coded cases [1].
- Delivery model. PR4 dependsOn RI12 "Delivery/business model/work culture" (DEP61): robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context [2], peer-reviewed. RI12 is drawn on by 16 of the 50 coded cases. [1] The same requirement reappears one level up: AT8 "Industrialised" dependsOn RI12 (DEP81), since adopting digital fabrication at industrialised scale depends on adapted business models [1].
- Off-site production. PR4 hasPrecondition PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site" (DEP55): automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials [1], peer-reviewed. PR2 is drawn on by 20 of the 50 coded cases. [1]
- Product standardisation and planning upstream of it. AT7 "Highly standardised" enablesCapability PR4 (DEP88), as Japanese automated erection systems rely on standardised prefabricated components [1], and PR12 "Path-planning" enablesCapability PR4 (DEP23), path planning being a precondition for robotic assembly [1]. AT7 is drawn on by 25 of the 50 coded cases and PR12 by 26. [1] A further enabler, CO12 "Mobile factory" enablesCapability PR4 (DEP42), on the ground that an all-weather cover allows welding and assembly to proceed in a normal manner even in rain [1], but CO12 is drawn on by only 1 of the 50 coded cases [1], an order of magnitude below the others and not a general prescription.

**What changes when people share the workspace**

CO6 "Human-robot interaction" is drawn on by 32 of the 50 coded cases [1], and it carries three outbound edges. CO6 dependsOn RI6 "Require workforce training" (DEP34), because the success of human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce [1], peer-reviewed; RI6 is drawn on by 44 of the 50 coded cases [1], the heaviest requirement in this material. CO6 dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern" (DEP45), on standards evidence: human-robot collaborative work depends on compliance with robot safety standards [1], and CO6 mitigates RI20 "Work safety concern" (DEP57), through power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits [1]. Note the direction: training and regulatory compliance are upstream requirements, while the safety gain is downstream of the interaction, not a precondition of it. RI18 is drawn on by 12 cases and RI20 by 13. [1]

**What changes in contracting and design sequence**

CO11 "Early contractor involvement" is drawn on by 14 of the 50 coded cases [1] and is the single strongest lever on the delivery side, with three outbound enabling edges, all peer-reviewed: to PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site" (DEP22), since integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party to be involved in the early design phase and a delivery method that does so should be selected [1]; to PR9 "DfMA for DFAB process" (DEP77), early collaboration being among the DfMA enablers [1]; and to AT12 "Integrated design-DFAB process" (DEP65), where BIM and early contractor involvement improve design management and increase DFAB adoption [1]. PR9 is drawn on by 15 cases. [1]

AT12 "Integrated design-DFAB process" is drawn on by 19 of the 50 coded cases [1], exactly the same number as AT11 "Sequential design-DFAB process" [1], so the integrated route is not yet the majority practice. It has its own organisational precondition: AT12 hasPrecondition CO10 "Vertical integration" (DEP35), because technically interdependent systems require tighter organisational coupling such as a single firm [1], with CO10 also running the other way as an enabler of AT12 (DEP64), though that corroborating edge is self-declared correlational [1]. CO10 is drawn on by 25 of the 50 coded cases. [1] A role change accompanies it: AC4 "DFAB design coordinator" enablesCapability AT12 (DEP85), interdisciplinary team integration linking actors to integrated design-DFAB processes [1], but AC4 is drawn on by only 8 of the 50 coded cases [1], against 39 of 50 for AC1 "DFAB engineer" [1]: projects staff the engineer far more readily than the coordinator.

Production control changes too: PR18 "Lean" hasPrecondition AR14 "Task schedule planning" (DEP99), since production with short takt requires a highly detailed definition of tasks to avoid ambiguousness [1]. PR18 is drawn on by 21 cases and AR14 by 28. [1]

**The cost of the change, and the return**

The standardisation this demands has a recorded downside: RI15 "Design compromise/over standardised" is drawn on by 17 of the 50 coded cases [1], and the offsetting flexibility claim is thin, AT7 enablesCapability VA21 [1]
